newsitem.title: UK: UK's Co-op gets substantial payment from Regan.
newsitem.headline: UK's Co-op gets substantial payment from Regan.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) won another moral victory in its legal battle against those responsible for the failed 1.2 million pound ($2 million) bid for it with a "substantial" out-of-court settlement.

City sources said the settlement of its civil claim against former CWS manager Allan Green, entrepreneur Andrew Regan and his business associate David Lyons and two companies involved in the bid had reached a million pounds.

CWS said in a statement that civil proceedings against Green, Regan, Lyons and Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica had now ended, although it will pursue its private criminal prosecution against Regan, Lyons and Green.

Regan's ambitious plan to takeover the 153-year-old supermarkets to funeral parlours group was scotched by a High Court injunction granted to the CWS preventing the use of confidential information leaked to Regan, Lyons, Lanica and Galileo by Green.

A preliminary hearing of the CWS private prosecution is due on May 26. Regan and Lyons have said they intend to "vigorously" defend the proceedings, a position re-iterated in a statement by Regan's Lanica Trust on Monday.

The CWS has already dropped legal action against investment bank Hambros and City law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite after both apologised unreservedly for their conduct. These settlements also involved a substantial financial element.

Both firms acted as advisers to Regan and Galileo in his abortive takeover attempt but along with most of the other institutions involved, including Schroder Investment Management, Jupiter Asset Management and stockbroker Killik & Co, have since distanced themselves from Regan.
Banking sources have suggested Hambros and Travers Smith Braithwaite could face legal action from Galileo's liquidator over the quality of advice given to Galileo.

Lanica, which said it invested 602,000 pounds in Galileo when it was formed in December 1996, said it had not been required to contribute to the payment to CWS "and accordingly has no financial exposure in respect of the action save for its own legal costs which are expected to be minimal".

"The liquidator of Galileo is considering bringing claims against certain former advisers to recover substantial damages. Lanica, as one of the shareholders in Galileo, may benefit if Galileo is successful in these claims," it added.

Lanica also revealed it would "shortly" announce the date on which it will publish its 1996 results. "It is anticipated that Lanica's listing can be restored at the time of the announcement of its results," the firm said.
Earlier this month Lanica, which had its shares suspended on the London Stock Exchange in February at 19.5 pounds each, said it would seek legal advice on the extent of its liability.

Lanica's shares were star performers in 1996, they staged a phenomenal rise after Regan took over when the stock was trading at 203 pence. But they were suspended on February 10 when it emerged Galileo was considering an approach to CWS.

The bid has been one of the most controversial in recent City memory, not only resulting in a humiliating climbdown for Hambros but also a Serious Fraud Office investigation into a previous deal between CWS and another Regan run company.

The SFO is investigating the circumstances of a controversial contract and a payment of 2.4 million pounds agreed in January 1995 between CWS and Regan's Hobson Group. CWS said it remained interested in the outcome of this probe. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
